name: Tar water

lead: Tar water is a drink made by steeping pine or fir tar in water. It was a medieval remedy, revived in the 18th century and again in the Victorian era, and promoted as a general tonic.
Its link to appearance is through historical use for skin and general health; its best-known advocate was the philosopher George Berkeley, who wrote about it in Siris in 1744.

paras: Historically the tar and water were stirred together, left to stand, and the separated water drunk, in doses of about half a pint morning and night per Berkeley. It was also used as a substitute for strong spirits.

Medical experts have regarded it as quackery, and it fell out of favour because of its taste. Tar-derived products can irritate, and modern safety data on drinking it do not exist in the sources consulted.

chain: Tar-steeped water drunk as a tonic
angle.text: Proponents offered tar water as an all-round tonic; any effect on looks was part of broad health claims rather than a defined cosmetic mechanism.

lead: Tar water is a remedy made from pine tar and water; it dates to medieval times, fell from favour because of its foul taste, was revived in the Victorian era, and was regarded by medical experts as quackery.[1]

The philosopher George Berkeley (1685-1753) championed it as a tonic and substitute for strong spirits in his 1744 tract Siris.[1] Physician Cadwallader Colden (1688-1776) promoted a similar pine-resin preparation.[1]

It is catalogued here among skin and wellness tonics because tonics of this sort were used for general complexion and health claims; literature on tar water also appears in nineteenth-century medical journals such as an 1873 piece on a new process and an 1880 article on its use in obstetrical and gynaecological practice.[2][3]

paras: Berkeley suggested stirring pine or fir tar with an equal amount of water for three or four minutes, letting it stand for 48 hours, and drinking the separated water, about half a pint morning and night on an empty stomach.[1]

Explorer Henry Ellis praised it against scurvy in 1746; his editor James Lind attributed the outbreak mainly to a lack of greens.[1] Henry Fielding tried it briefly for dropsy in 1749.[1] Dickens used it in Great Expectations (1861) as a cruel punishment inflicted on Pip.[1]
Nineteenth-century medical journals still discussed it, including a 1873 article on a new process and an 1880 article on obstetrical and gynaecological use.[2][3]
Medical experts have regarded tar water as quackery.[1]
No studies found. Modern PubMed hits for the term concern unrelated industrial tar-water mixtures.
